html:
An Indian painter from Travancore, in today's Kerala, who lived from 1848 to 1906. He joined European oil painting to Indian subjects, and his prints gave India its popular images of gods and heroes.

Born into an aristocratic family connected to the Travancore royal house, he learned oil painting largely on his own, with some help from a visiting European portraitist. He painted portraits for Indian princes and British officials, and won prizes at exhibitions in India and abroad.

He is best known for scenes from the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and classical poetry: Shakuntala writing a love letter, Damayanti and the swan, goddesses such as Lakshmi and Saraswati. He gave them realistic bodies, rich saris and Indian settings.

In 1894 he opened a lithographic press near Bombay that printed cheap colour copies of his pictures. They spread into homes, shrines, calendars and shops across India. His style of gods shaped later calendar art, film and comics. Critics later called his work too Western, and the Progressive Artists' Group turned away from it, but he remains one of the most famous Indian artists.
